entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17309"/><div sID="gen34498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17309"/><hi type="bold">10. advice--</hi>Herein he does not (as some misinterpret the passage) disclaim inspiration for the advice he gives; but under the Spirit, states that it is his "opinion" [Alford] or "judgment" [Ellicott, and others], not a command, that so their offering might be free and spontaneous.<div eID="gen34498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this--</hi>my giving you an advice, not a command.<div eID="gen34499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who have begun before--</hi>"seeing that ye have begun before" the Macedonian churches; "a year ago" should be connected with this clause.<div eID="gen34500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not only to do, but also to be forward--</hi>There were three steps: (1) the forwardness, more literally, "the will"; (2) the setting about it, literally, "doing it"; (3) completion of it [Alford]. In the two former, not only the act, but the intention, the Corinthians preceded the Macedonians. Bengel explains, "Not only to do" FOR THE PAST YEAR, "but also to be forward" or willing FOR THIS YEAR. Ellicott translates, "already," instead of "before": "Ye began already a year ago, not only to do, but also to be forward." It appears hence, that something had been done in the matter a year before; other texts, however, show the collection was not yet paid (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.11">2Co 8:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.5">2Co 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">7</reference>). This agrees with one, and only one supposition, namely, that every man had laid by in store the fund from which he was afterwards to contribute, the very case which is shown by <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1Co 16:2</reference> to have existed [Paley, Horæ Paulinæ]. <div eID="gen34501" type="x-p"/>

For--</hi>Following up the rule "out of that which ye have" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.11">2Co 8:11</reference>), and no more.<div eID="gen34505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a willing mind--</hi>rather, as Greek, "the readiness," namely, to will, referring to <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.11">2Co 8:11</reference>.<div eID="gen34506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">accepted--</hi>Greek "favorably accepted."<div eID="gen34507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to that a man hath--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "a man." Translate, "According to whatsoever it have"; the willing mind, or "readiness" to will, is personified [Alford]. Or better, as Bengel, "He is accepted according to whatsoever he have"; so <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">2Co 9:7</reference>, The Lord loveth a cheerful giver." Compare as to David, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.18">1Ki 8:18</reference>. God accepts the will for the deed. He judges not according to what a man has the opportunity to do, but according to what he would do if he had the opportunity (compare <reference osisRef="Mark.14.8">Mr 14:8</reference>; and the widow's mite, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.3">Lu 21:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.4">4</reference>). <div eID="gen34508" type="x-p"/>

Or better, as Bengel, "He is accepted according to whatsoever he have"; so 2Co 9:7 , The Lord loveth a cheerful giver." Compare as to David, 1Ki 8:18 . God accepts the will for the deed. He judges not according to what a man has the opportunity to do, but according to what he would do if he had the opportunity (compare Mr 14:8 ; and the widow's mite, Lu 21:3 , 4 ).

entries.reader_content_plain: 13. For-- Supply from 2Co 8:8 , "I speak." My aim is not that others (namely, the saints at Jerusalem) may be relieved at the cost of your being "distressed" (so the Greek for "burdened"). The golden rule is, "Love thy neighbour as thyself," not more than thyself.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17313"/><div sID="gen34510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17313"/><hi type="bold">14. by an equality--</hi>"by the rule of equality" [Alford]: literally, "Out of equality."<div eID="gen34510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now at this time--</hi>Greek, "at the present juncture" or season.<div eID="gen34511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that their abundance also--</hi>The Greek being distinct from the previous "that," translate, "in order that," namely, at another season, when your relative circumstances may be reversed. The reference is solely to temporal wants and supplies. Those, as Bengel, who quote <reference osisRef="Rom.15.27">Ro 15:27</reference> for interpreting it of spiritual supplies from the Jews to the Gentiles, forget that <reference osisRef="Rom.15.27">Ro 15:27</reference> refers to the past benefit spiritually, which the Jews have conferred on the Gentiles, as a motive to gratitude on the part of the latter, not to a prospective benefit to be looked for from the former, which the text refers to. <div eID="gen34512" type="x-p"/>

(<reference osisRef="Exod.16.18">Ex 16:18</reference>; Septuagint). As God gave an equal portion of manna to all the Israelites, whether they could gather much or little; so Christians should promote by liberality an equality, so that none should need the necessaries of life while others have superfluities. "Our luxuries should yield to our neighbor's comforts; and our comforts to his necessities" [J. Howard]. <div eID="gen34513" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17317"/><div sID="gen34518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17317"/><hi type="bold">18. the brother, whose praise is in the gospel--</hi>whose praise is known in connection with the Gospel: Luke may be meant; not that "the Gospel" here refers to his written Gospel; but the language implies some one well known throughout the churches, and at that time with Paul, as Luke then was (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.6">Ac 20:6</reference>). Not a Macedonian, as appears from <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.4">2Co 9:4</reference>. Of all Paul's "companions in travel" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.19">2Co 8:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.19.29">Ac 19:29</reference>), Luke was the most prominent, having been his companion in preaching the Gospel at his first entrance into Europe (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.10">Ac 16:10</reference>). The fact that the person here referred to was "chosen of the churches" as their trustee to travel with Paul in conveying the contribution to Jerusalem, implies that he had resided among them some time before: this is true of Luke, who after parting from Paul at Philippi (as he marks by the change from "we" to "they," <reference osisRef="Acts.16.11">Ac 16:11</reference>) six years before, is now again found in his company in Macedonia. In the interim he had probably become so well known that "his praise was throughout all the churches." Compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.18">2Co 12:18</reference>; Phm 24. He who is faithful in the Gospel will be faithful also in matters of inferior importance [Bengel]. <div eID="gen34518" type="x-p"/>

Not a Macedonian, as appears from 2Co 9:4 . Of all Paul's "companions in travel" ( 2Co 8:19 ; Ac 19:29 ), Luke was the most prominent, having been his companion in preaching the Gospel at his first entrance into Europe ( Ac 16:10 ). In the interim he had probably become so well known that "his praise was throughout all the churches." Compare 2Co 12:18 ; Phm 24. He who is faithful in the Gospel will be faithful also in matters of inferior importance [Bengel].

This and the previous clause, "to the glory of the same Lord," do not follow "administered by us," but "chosen of the churches to travel," &c. The union of the brother with Paul in this affair of the collection was done to guard against suspicions injurious "to the glory" of the Lord.
